extraction_needs.data: the per-layer hidden embeddings e_{l,t} of the alignment batch, with their place in the autograd graph
extraction_needs.where: inside the forward pass of an alignment step, server side
extraction_needs.via: ModelHandle.activations(samples, select, pool, what) returns each selected module's input or output, but at pool="none" only for 3-D activations and always .detach()ed, so the tensors are readable and not differentiable; nothing returns them with a graph.

extraction_needs.data: the gradient of the alignment loss with respect to each layer's hidden embedding, dL/de_l
extraction_needs.where: after the first backward of an alignment step, before the second forward
extraction_needs.via: no interface reaches layer outputs. LossView.gradients_of(scalar, select) computes torch.autograd.grad against named_parameters() only, and ModelHandle.per_sample_gradients differentiates per sample against a parameter group (or frozen base weights under scope="all"); a hidden activation is neither.

extraction_needs.data: a forward pass of the same batch with a perturbation added to each layer's output (f_wl(e) + eps_l)
extraction_needs.where: the second pass of an alignment step
extraction_needs.via: ModelHandle has no hook, patch or pre-forward method, and the plugin contract forbids reaching past the handle. The trainer extension states the same limit from the other side ("What stays out of reach: the forward pass itself ... intermediate activations"); its transform_loss action replaces the loss scalar after the pass, which cannot change what the pass computed. loss_on(batch)/losses(samples) run the model's own forward on samples and accept no activations.

extraction_needs.data: the alignment mini-batch (x_t, y_t) of the provider's own corpus
extraction_needs.where: every alignment optimization step, before the first forward
extraction_needs.via: LossView.loss_on(batch) and HFModelHandle accept a batch in the trainer's format, and hf_trainer_ext.collate_texts builds one from texts, so a defender-supplied corpus can be turned into a batch. But this only reaches the loss, i.e. the same forward-pass limit as above; and the paper's placement is pre-deployment, before any user data or client exists, so no client-side ALIGNMENT batch exists unless one declares the federation step itself to be the alignment.

extraction_needs.data: the global cross-layer gradient norm ||concat_l dL/de_l||
extraction_needs.where: between the first backward and the perturbation construction
extraction_needs.via: follows from dL/de_l: with no per-layer gradients there is nothing to concatenate. Note the normalization is over all layers at once; a per-layer norm would be a different (and wrong) method.

extraction_needs.data: an optimizer step driven by the gradient of the perturbed pass
extraction_needs.via: the host owns the optimizer; fedguard's only gradient point is CLIENT_PRE_STEP ('gradients are computed, the optimizer has not stepped'), which can replace a gradient but cannot supply one produced by a second, differently-corrupted forward pass.

extraction_needs.data: the trainable LoRA factors the alignment updates, and their merge into the base model
extraction_needs.via: states.* and the LoRA state dicts are the library's normal currency, and SERVER_DISTRIBUTE/outgoing carry the model that is sent; the merge itself is a training-run operation, not a per-round intervention.

external_state: the provider's safety alignment corpus {x_i, y_i} (the paper uses 2000 BeaverTails harmful-prompt/safe-answer pairs): a `resources` entry, never a fedguard view

the pre-trained LLM being aligned, and a server-side model handle to run it: a server-side plugin may declare `model_handle`, but the host supplies no model on the server, so the defender must pass one in
the alignment optimizer and its schedule (AdamW, lr 1e-3, weight decay 0.1, cosine decay, warmup 0.1) plus the T-step / 50-epoch loop: the host's training loop, outside any plugin
the LoRA adapters (rank 8, dropout 0.1), one for alignment and one for later user fine-tuning, and the merge step between them
the user fine-tuning stage itself, which Vaccine deliberately leaves untouched (Appendix E)

missing_runtime.what: a differentiable read of a layer's output (hidden embedding) with a graph, at a point where the loss is available
missing_runtime.blocks: step 2 (backward_layer_embedding_grad) and therefore step 3 (concat_layer_gradient_norm) and step 4 (layerwise_embedding_perturbation)

missing_runtime.what: a way to run one forward pass with a supplied modification to a layer's output, i.e. a plugin-visible forward hook or a handle that accepts perturbed activations
missing_runtime.blocks: step 5 (forward_hook_add_perturbation) and step 6 (perturbed_forward_backward), which is the entire defense: without it Vaccine degenerates into ordinary SFT (the paper's own point 3)

missing_runtime.what: a training-step position on the server side, where this one-off alignment actually happens; the server has no model and no step, and the client-side steps run after their host's forward pass has finished
missing_runtime.blocks: steps 1-7 as an alignment stage; only a client-side ALIGNMENT step would be reachable, which is a different method

missing_runtime.what: a loss point whose forward pass has not already been consumed, i.e. an extension that can re-enter the model rather than only replace the loss scalar
missing_runtime.blocks: the whole two-pass structure; transform_loss at CLIENT_LOSS substitutes a scalar but cannot inject anything into the pass that produced it

deviations: The paper is centralized (no clients, no round, no aggregation) and runs once at alignment time, before any user fine-tuning. A fedguard plugin is invoked at fixed points of a federated round; the nearest intended position is server-side before distribution (SERVER_DISTRIBUTE), which is why the shell is mounted there. This placement had to be chosen by the port, not read off the paper.

The paper's mechanism (steps 2-6) is not ported at all: it is not expressible with the published interfaces. No substitute was fabricated, because a gradient-level stand-in (after-the-fact scaling of CLIENT_PRE_STEP gradients) is not what the paper does: the paper's own point 3 is that one pass degenerates to ordinary SFT.

The method needs a model on the server, but the host supplies none; a server-side plugin may declare `model_handle` and have the defender pass one in, which is a deployment requirement recorded under `external_state`, not something this port can supply.

Nothing of the method's numeric settings (rho, batch 5, 50 epochs, lr 1e-3, AdamW, weight decay 0.1, LoRA rank 8 / dropout 0.1) is baked into the shell, since none of it could be exercised; the report's numbers are the paper's, not this port's.
open_choices: the default rho for the main experiments (Section 5.1 gives none; Tables 6 and 7 sweep 0.01/0.1/1/2/5/10, and Section 5.4 mentions 0.2, which no table lists) — nothing chosen, since the mechanism is unported
how to treat a zero or near-zero cross-layer gradient norm, where eps = rho * g / ||g|| is undefined: the paper gives no stability rule (an eps floor or a skipped step would have to be chosen)

whether the perturbation covers every token position, every hidden dimension, and modules beyond attention (the algorithm says each layer l in L, 4.2 says LoRA on the attention modules) — not resolvable from the text
whether the first backward uses retain_graph or a second forward pass to keep the embedding gradients (the paper does not say)
the Double-LoRA description versus Appendix B.1's 'we use the same LoRA adaptor for alignment/fine-tuning'
how T relates to 50 epochs, batch size 5 and 2000 samples (drop-last, gradient accumulation)
the default tau and how to choose it for accelerated Vaccine (Table 10 gives four points, no rule)
random seeds, repetition count and error bars (the paper gives none)
how Vaccine would extend to RLHF (Appendix E lists it as a limitation)
how alignment results would be combined across clients if this were moved into a federated setting: the paper is silent and this port cannot invent it
needs_from_authors: whether the reference implementation keeps embedding gradients with retain_graph or with two independent forward passes, and its numerical guard when the gradient norm is zero (dictates whether a future interface needs graph retention or just a repeatable forward)

whether the perturbation is applied to attention-only modules or to every block output, and whether it covers all token positions and hidden dimensions (decides which module outputs an interface would have to expose)
the default rho and the intended way to select it, absent from Section 5.1
whether the alignment and fine-tuning adapters are the same object or two, given the conflict between 4.2 and Appendix B.1
confidence_reason: The negative finding is solid and rests on interfaces I read in the tree, not on inference: ModelHandle (fedguard/views/model.py) has no hook or forward-patch method and its activations() returns detached tensors; LossView.gradients_of (fedguard/views/client.py) differentiates only against named_parameters(); the trainer extension's own docstring names the forward pass and intermediate activations as out of reach, and its transform_loss action can only replace the scalar after the pass. The verdict is capped below high because it is an argument about a missing capability, which cannot be confirmed by a test, and because I could not execute anything to check it: the standing policy is read-only and no writable temp directory exists, so importing torch fails and the escalation for a scratch directory found no approval channel. I therefore verified by reading source and left the working tree untouched (git status on fedguard/ is clean). If a hidden path to the model (or a plugin that ignores the ModelHandle contract) were accepted, step 2 could be reached; step 5, the injection, has no such path at all, which is what fixes the verdict.
